newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Ecuador's Bucaram concedes defeat, vows comeback.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador's Bucaram concedes defeat, vows comeback.

text.p: Ecuador's ousted president Abdala Bucaram, saying he was deposed with the tacit support of the military, reluctantly conceded defeat on Sunday but vowed to make a political comeback.

Bucaram -- a 44-year-old fiery populist who enraged his impoverished nation with economic belt-tightening measures aimed at cutting fat where there was only bone -- said Ecuadoreans would soon regret his dismissal after just six months in office.

In a rambling and often incomprehensible live interview on national television in the middle of the night, Bucaram admitted defeat for the first time since Congress dismissed him as president three days earlier in a no-confidence vote citing alleged mental incompetence.

"If you think I'm crazy today just wait to see what kind of craziness is coming in the future," Bucaram, who is popularly known as "El Loco" or "madman," told Ecuavisa television from his home in the Pacific coast city of Guayaquil.
"I'm going to be a candidate for the presidency in the next elections," he said.
Bucaram, of Lebanese origin, was the third South American president to be ousted since 1992.

Like Venezuela's Carlos Andres Perez, who was forced to step down in 1993 after trying to impose harsh austerity measures, he maintained that he was a victim of conspiracy and hardball politics Latin-style.
"This is the dictatorship of the national Congress," he said, insisting that while he remained the duly elected president he had effectively been stripped of all ability to rule.

"This is something unheard of in history," he added, referring to an agreement worked out between lawmakers and the country's powerful military leaders late on Saturday clearing the way for a solution of the deepening constitutional crisis.
Legislators and top military officials agreed on a plan allowing Vice President Rosalia Arteaga, 40, to take over as interim president.

But Ecuador's first woman president was certain to serve even less time on the job than Bucaram. Congressional leader Fabian Alarcon was initally voted by Congress to replace Bucaram, but legal questions arose over the ability of Congress to unilaterally select a replacement president.
Congress was expected to pass new legislation next week that would allit it to reappoint Alarcon as president.

Accusing the military of "having intervened politically," Bucaram said the high command had allowed Congress to "usurp" power from a sitting president, who was inexplicably never given the right to defend himself in a full-blown impeachment trial.
"Congress is not a psychiatrist," Bucaram said.

His embittered remarks followed the resignation of his defence minister early on Saturday and a subsequent statement from a respected army general confirming that the military had basically pulled the rug out from under his government.

Bucaram was ousted after a crippling strike that shut down most of Ecuador for two days last week. The strike was called to protest austerity measures ordered in January by the same man who promised during last year's campaign to champion Ecuador's overwhelming majority of poor people.

His antics in public, including a luncheon with Ecuadorean-American Lorena Bobbit of penis-slashing infamy, did little to curry favour with Ecuador's elite, and neither did the singing career he launched soon after taking office.

In his TV interview he insisted that Ecuadoreans would be demanding his return to the presidential palace within a month because the "congressional coup" was a miscarriage of justice and would shake international confidence in Ecuador's democratic institutions.
"International credits will be withdrawn," he predicted, adding that the de facto government would have "no legitimacy to govern with" and could fall apart within 40 days.
The unprecedented constitutional crisis stemmed not just from Bucaram's refusal to step down but also from claims by Arteaga and Alarcon that both had legal rights to succeeed him.

The deal apparently ending the crisis, announced on the floor of Congress early on Sunday, would see Alarcon serving as interim head of state until August 1998, when he would step down in the aftermath of extraordinary elections early next year.
Arteaga will only step down, to reassume the vice presidency, after lawmakers plug a key loophole in the constitution that failed to spell out who replaces sitting a president.
